committeeQuestion.scholarship: Why should we invest in this student?
committeeQuestion.grant: Why should we invest in this project, and can the team deliver?

items: I meet the nationality, residency, age, academic-level and subject requirements
Committees reject ineligible applications without reading them. Check each condition against the official call.
I meet the minimum GPA or class and the language-proficiency score
Minimum scores are usually hard cut-offs. Make sure your test date leaves time for results.
I've checked the eligible expenses and any funding restrictions
Knowing what the award will and won't pay for avoids budget errors and unrealistic plans.
I've confirmed the deadline, submission method and required file formats
Late or wrongly formatted submissions are a common, avoidable reason for rejection.
I understand the funder's mission, priorities and published selection criteria
Reviewers score against published criteria. Mirror their priorities with your evidence.
My application is tailored to this funder, with no generic statements
Generic statements signal low commitment. Name the funder's goals and show how you match them.
I can explain why this specific scholarship or grant fits my goals
A clear fit argument answers the core question: why invest in you, here, now.
My transcripts, GPA, class ranking and awards are presented accurately
Inconsistencies between transcripts and claims undermine trust in the whole application.
My relevant qualifications and certifications are included
Relevant certifications strengthen the evidence that you are ready for the programme.
It explains why this opportunity matters to me
Motivation is usually weighted heavily for scholarships. Be specific rather than sentimental.
It connects my past experience, current goals and future plans into one clear story
A connected story helps reviewers remember you among hundreds of applicants.
It links the opportunity to my academic, research and career goals
Showing where this opportunity leads makes the investment case concrete.
I describe my contributions and results, not just a list of activities
Committees look for the impact you created, not memberships.
I give measurable achievements: outcomes, publications, competitions, presentations and documented contributions
Numbers and documented outputs make achievements verifiable.
The title and abstract summarise the question, approach and intended outcomes
Many reviewers form a view from the abstract alone. Make the question and approach obvious.
The background and rationale explain the problem and why it matters
A strong rationale shows the problem matters beyond your own interest.
I state a clear research gap and objectives I can achieve
A precise gap and achievable objectives show you understand the field.
I explain what is novel and significant
Originality is usually a top criterion for research funding.
The methodology is suitable and sound: design, data, tools, analysis and validation
Sound methods convince reviewers the project can produce valid results.
The work plan has realistic milestones and deliverables
Realistic milestones show you can deliver within the funding period.
The budget is itemised, justified and follows the funder's rules
Budgets that break funder rules often fail at the compliance stage.
I define the expected outcomes and a plan for sharing the findings
Funders want results used. A dissemination plan shows reach beyond the thesis.
I describe the team, supervision and institutional support
Supervision and institutional backing reassure reviewers that the work can be delivered.
I cover ethics approvals, risks, mitigation and sustainability
Unaddressed ethics or risk concerns can stop an otherwise strong proposal.
My referees know my work and can give specific examples
Specific examples from referees carry more weight than general praise.
My referees have agreed to write and know the deadline
Late references can leave an application incomplete. Give referees at least three to four weeks.
I can explain the problem being addressed and who benefits
Committees fund change. Name the problem and the people who benefit.
I name tangible outputs: publications, datasets, prototypes or recommendations
Tangible outputs make impact measurable and credible.
I explain how I will use the knowledge and skills I gain
Showing how you will apply your skills answers the long-term value question.
All supporting documents are complete, accurate and correctly formatted
Missing or mislabelled documents can disqualify an application at screening.
Every claim is accurate and sources are acknowledged where required
Misstatements can lead to an offer being withdrawn, even after award.
A supervisor, mentor or experienced grant writer has reviewed my draft
An experienced reader spots gaps you can no longer see in your own draft.
The final application follows every funder instruction
Word limits, file names and formats are often checked before content is read.
